In the printed tradition, are the accents of the Decalogue grammatical?

The question

Roughly speaking, each Decalogue has two strands of cantillation, the טעם תחתון and the טעם עליון. Why is this only roughly true? Because in detail there are four strands: the printed tradition (p-trad) and the manuscript tradition (m-trad) differ in cantillation, yielding two different עליון strands and two different תחתון strands. (The p-trad is fading, but still visible in editions like Koren and Simanim's Tiqqun.) The most striking difference between the four strands is how they divide up the span אנכי…מצותי into chanted verses. (This span is typically identified as comprising the first two Commandments.)

I have run Richard Goerwitz's accent grammar checker against the m-trad strands (as represented by WLC); this page shows what happens when the checker is run against the p-trad strands.

There is no dual cantillation to detangle here. Whereas the Tiberian manuscripts (and WLC) pack both of their strands onto one set of letters, the Wikisource page עשרת הדברות בסיס/טעמים spells out all the strands separately — p-trad and m-trad alike — each as single cantillation. Every chanted verse (delimited by its own sof pasuq) is grammar-checked on its own. The m-trad is the baseline — MAM's own authoritative text, expected to parse clean throughout — and the p-trad is the object of study.

The verdict

m-trad versesp-trad verses
Ex. תחתון✓ all 12 clean✓ all 13 clean
Ex. עליון✓ all 10 clean✗ 1 of 9 ungrammatical (verse 1)
Deut. תחתון✓ all 12 clean✓ all 13 clean
Deut. עליון✓ all 10 clean✗ 1 of 9 ungrammatical (verse 1)

The תחתון is grammatical everywhere — both books, both traditions. In terms of verse boundaries, the p-trad תחתון differs from the m-trad in only one place: the p-trad תחתון ends its first verse at מבית עבדים (so it has one more verse than the m-trad, whose first verse runs on to על־פני instead). Both parse clean. It also differs in some further details — several of them changes of cantillation that give the two strands genuinely different parses, but none that costs either its grammaticality (catalogued in an appendix below).

The עליון is grammatical in the m-trad but not in the p-trad: the p-trad עליון of each Decalogue has exactly one ungrammatical chanted verse — its opening one.

The four strands of אנכי…עבדים

The m-trad and p-trad accent the Decalogue's אנכי…עבדים span differently. The accent on עבדים is what decides the structure: a silluq + sof pasuq there ends the verse, so אנכי…עבדים stands as its own verse; an etnaḥta or revia there is mid-verse, folding אנכי…עבדים into a longer verse. The table below lays all four strands over the same milestone words — אנכי (their common start), then עבדים, על־פני, and מצותי — so their subset relation is plain: every verse starts green at אנכי and ends red at its own last word, the shorter ones stopping where the longer ones keep going. Each strand keeps its own accent on עבדים, the structure-deciding mark:

mTאנכי֙עבד֑יםעל־פנֽי׃
mE/pTאנכ֖יעבדֽים׃
pEאנכי֙עבד֗יםעל־פנ֗ימצותֽי׃
  • P-trad תחתון = m-trad עליון — but only in the first chanted verse, where the table gives them a single shared row, labelled mE/pT. The equality stops there: past this first verse the two strands diverge — the p-trad תחתון divides each Decalogue into 13 chanted verses, the m-trad עליון into only 10.
  • P-trad עליון ≠ m-trad עליון. The p-trad עליון puts revia on עבדים and runs the first two commandments together into one verse, leading to only 9 chanted verses total. In contrast, the first chanted verse of the m-trad's עליון ends on עבדים, leading to 10 chanted verses total.
  • The m-trad תחתון does not give אנכי…עבדים its own verse either — it runs אנכי…פני together (etnaḥta at עבדים, sof pasuq at פני), a third structure again.

Of these four strands, only the p-trad עליון is ungrammatical — the verdict above already said so — and the section below dissects its merged opening verse.

Why the p-trad עליון fails: the merged first verse

As the four-strands table above laid out, in the m-trad עליון the first commandment אנכי…עבדים is its own chanted verse, and לא יהיה לך אלהים אחרים begins the next — two separate verses, both of which parse clean. The p-trad instead merges the first two commandments into a single verse. That one merged verse is what the grammar rejects. Shown stripped to letters and accents and divided at the p-trad תחתון's verse boundaries — one p-trad עליון verse (pE) spanning the five ordinary p-trad תחתון verses (pT) it merges:

pEאנכי֙…עבד֗יםל֣א יהיה־לך֩…על־פנ֗יל֣א תעשה־לך֣…לא֗רץלא־תשתחו֣ה…לשנא֑יוע֤שה…מצותֽי׃
pTאנכ֖י…עבדֽים׃לא־יהי֥ה לך֛…על־פנֽי׃לא־תעש֨ה לך֥…לאֽרץ׃לא־תשתחו֥ה…לשנאֽי׃וע֥שה…מצותֽי׃
pe
pt

The single etnaḥta falls at לשנאי, leaving a first half crowded with a segolta plus three separate revia domains (at עבדים, על־פני, and לארץ); the prose grammar cannot build it and returns a pashta_phrase error — the same failure, at the same structural point, in both Decalogues.

The cause is the merged structure, not sheer length: Deuteronomy's p-trad עליון Sabbath verse runs 55 words and parses clean, while this merged verse (51 words) does not. Keeping the two commandments as the m-trad's two separate verses (9 and 42 words) is exactly what lets them parse.

A tidier nesting — until you scrutinize it

It is tempting to call the p-trad's arrangement the neater one. Its five תחתון verses nest perfectly inside a single עליון verse — a clean five-in-one — whereas the m-trad divides the very same words into two עליון verses and four תחתון verses that do not nest cleanly at all: the m-trad תחתון's opening verse אנכי…על־פני straddles the עליון's break after עבדים, so neither strand's verses sit wholly inside the other's. In the gradient bars below, mE's first break lands inside mT's first verse, which runs on to על־פני — that is the straddle:

mEאנכ֖י…עבדֽים׃ל֣א יהיה־לך֩…על־פנ֗יל֣א תעשה־לך֣…לא֗רץלא־תשתחו֣ה…לשנא֑יוע֤שה…מצותֽי׃
mTאנכי֙…עבד֑יםלא־יהי֥ה לך֛…על־פנֽי׃לא־תעש֨ה לך֥…לאֽרץ׃לא־תשתחו֥ה…לשנאֽי׃וע֥שה…מצותֽי׃
me
mt

But the p-trad's tidiness is bought with an ungrammatical cantillation — the very one dissected above. Once you see the accents that buy the five-in-one, its neatness evaporates. This is not to say the tidier nesting could not have been cantillated grammatically; perhaps some other accentuation would have carried it off. That is a theoretical question I am not prepared to settle here.

Source

All eight strands (two books × תחתון/עליון × m-trad/p-trad) are taken from the Wikisource base page עשרת הדברות בסיס/טעמים (revision 2810844, 2023-10-22), which every p-trad-vs-m-trad comparison table there transcludes. A handful of wiki templates are resolved to plain pointed text (legarmeh and paseq both conflated down to a Unicode PASEQ, qere for ketiv-qere, setumah and petuḥah divisions dropped); the chanted verses are split at sof pasuq.

See also this document on the Decalogues in the Simanim Tiqqun — its main Decalogue uses the p-trad עליון and its appendix Decalogue the p-trad תחתון.

See also this document on the Decalogues in the Koren Tanakh — it has the p-trad תחתון in its Exodus main Decalogue and the p-trad עליון in its appendix Decalogue.

Appendix: how the two תחתון strands differ

Both תחתון strands parse clean everywhere, so the differences below do not bear on the grammaticality question this page asks — not even the several that do change the parse. They are gathered here only to make concrete the verdict's point that the strands differ in ways that never cost either strand grammaticality. The one structural difference — the p-trad ending its first verse at מבית עבדים, and the boundary accents on אנכי, אלהיך, מבית, and עבדים that follow from it — is the verdict's own point and is not repeated here.

In Exodus the two strands differ in essentially one grammar-irrelevant respect: the vocalization of לא תרצח — תִּרְצָ֖ח (m-trad, qamats) against תִּרְצַ֖ח (p-trad, patax). Both have the same tipeḥa; only the vowel differs.

Deuteronomy differs in more ways. Three are differences of cantillation — which, unlike the Exodus vowel-swap, do change the parse — and all three fall within a single stretch of the Sabbath commandment. Below is just that stretch — the run of words the two strands accent differently, everything before and after it being identical — shown in each strand, m-trad above p-trad, stripped to letters and accents, each line ending on a disjunctive accent:

m-tradל֣א תעש֣ה כל־מלאכ֡ה
p-tradלא־תעש֨ה כל־מלאכ֜ה
m-tradאת֣ה ובנך־ובת֣ך ועבדך־ו֠אמת֠ך
p-tradאת֣ה׀ ובנך־ובת֣ך ועבדך־ואמת֗ך
m-tradושורך֨ וחמרך֜ וכל־בהמת֗ך
p-tradושורך֤ וחמרך֙ וכל־בהמת֔ך

Two further differences are purely vocalization — vowel-pointing, not cantillation:

  • The same תִּרְצָ֖ח / תִּרְצַ֖ח split as in Exodus.
  • Qamats qatan vs. plain qamats. Two words the m-trad points with qamats qatan but the p-trad with plain qamats — כׇל / וְכׇל against כָל / וְכָל. This one is not a real m-trad/p-trad difference at all, but a defect in the source — its own Exodus תחתון points the same words with qamats qatan. Reported as MAM-basics issue #202.

A p-trad Bible on the web: CTR

Possibly the only p-trad Bible on the web is CTR: a web version of The Complete Tanach with Rashi, served from Chabad.org. CTR has not only the characteristic opening verse of the p-trad תחתון but also the p-trad תחתון accents in the Sabbath commandment.

For more on CTR: see my review, which calls it “certainly the weirdest Hebrew Bible on the web, and possibly the worst.”
